title: Backtracking
summary: Systematic search technique that builds solutions step by step, drills down, and backtracks when a partial solution cannot be extended to a valid solution. It includes modeling such as n-tuple, decision tree, feasibility pruning, general scheme, N-Queens 4×4, complexity analysis and comparison with brute force and greedy algorithms.

learningObjectives.text: Define backtracking as systematic depth exploration with backtracking and pruning.
Model a solution as an n-tuple where each component is chosen from a finite set of candidates.
Build the decision tree associated with a backtracking problem.
Identify the meaning of a partial solution and a state of the tree.
Apply pruning when a partial solution cannot be extended to a valid solution.
Distinguish backtracking from brute force by when invalid branches are discarded.
Distinguish backtracking from voracious algorithms by the reversibility of decisions.
Solve N-Queens 4×4 by incremental construction and pruning by columns and diagonals.
Analyze backtracking complexity based on the size of the search tree and the cost of validating candidates.
Recognize classic problems solvable with backtracking: N-Queens, sum of subsets, graph coloring, Sudoku and restricted permutations.

terms.label: Backtracking
terms.definition: Search technique that builds incremental solutions and backtracks when it detects that the partial solution cannot lead to a valid solution.

terms.label: Decision tree
terms.definition: Tree where each level represents a stage of the problem and each branch represents a possible choice.

terms.label: Partial solution
terms.definition: Incomplete assignment of decisions, for example (x0, x1, ..., xk, ?, ..., ?).

terms.label: Solutions space
terms.definition: Set of all possible combinations before applying constraints or pruning.

terms.label: Candidate
terms.definition: Possible value to complete the next position of the partial solution.

terms.label: Feasibility
terms.definition: Condition that determines whether a partial solution still respects the constraints of the problem.

terms.label: Pruning
terms.definition: Removing a branch from the search tree because it cannot lead to a valid solution.

terms.label: Recoil
terms.definition: Action of undoing a decision and returning to the previous state to try another candidate.

terms.label: DFS
terms.definition: Depth-First Search or depth search. Backtracking explores a branch to the bottom before turning back.

terms.label: Live node
terms.definition: Tree node that can still be explored.

terms.label: Dead node
terms.definition: Node that is no longer explored because it is invalid, has already been completed, or can no longer produce a solution.

chapters.title: Backtracking
chapters.summary: Modeling solutions such as n-tuples, DFS exploration, feasibility pruning and complete N-Queens example.

learningObjectives.text: Understand the idea of moving forward, detecting blockage and moving back.
Understand that backtracking avoids exploring impossible branches before completing them.

content.text: Backtracking is a systematic search technique. It builds a solution step by step, tests candidates, and rolls back as soon as it detects that the partial solution can no longer be converted into a valid solution.
The exploration is done in depth. First an attempt is made to complete a branch of the decision tree. If the branch fails, it goes back to the previous level and tries the next candidate.
Backtracking does not prevent the problem from being combinatorial. What it does is not waste time completing combinations that are already impossible from an intermediate stage.

Xk is an incomplete solution that already has values assigned up to position k. Question marks (?) indicate decisions that have not yet been made.

learningObjectives.text: Read the general recursive backtracking scheme.
Differentiate the operations of choose, validate, advance and undo.

content.text: The basic pattern is recursive: if the solution is complete, it is reported; If not, candidates are tested for the next position. Each valid candidate opens a recursive call. Upon returning, the decision is undone.

learningObjectives.text: Model N-Queens as a vector of columns per row.
Reduce the search space by using one queen per row.

content.text: The problem of the N-Queens is to locate
queens on a board
without two queens attacking each other. Two queens attack each other if they share a row, column or diagonal.

Since there cannot be two queens in the same row, exactly one queen is placed per row. So the decision for each level is no longer choosing any square on the board, but rather choosing the column for the current row.

blocks.title: Solution model
blocks.latex: X=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),\qquad x_i=\text{columna de la reina en la fila }i

content.text: In this vector X, the index i represents the row of the board and the value xi represents the column where we place the queen of that row.
For each row, the Si candidates are simply the column numbers 1 through n.

The function checks that column c is not repeated and that there are no diagonal attacks. The formula |i-r| != |c-xr| It ensures that the distance in rows is not equal to the distance in columns, which characterizes diagonals.
The condition i=n+1 means that we have already managed to place a queen in each of the n rows of the board.

learningObjectives.text: Analyze the cost of backtracking as the size of the search tree.
Distinguish the worst case bound from the practical improvement by pruning.

content.text: The complexity of backtracking depends on the number of nodes visited in the search tree and the cost of validating each candidate. Pruning can reduce the actual work a lot, but the worst case is still combinatorial.
Nk is the number of nodes visited at level k of the tree and Cvalidar is the cost of running the feasibility function at that level.

blocks.title: Worst case with uniform branching factor
blocks.latex: T(d)=\begin{cases}\Theta(b^d\cdot C_{validar}),& \text{si se visitan casi todas las ramas}\\\Theta(N_{visitados}\cdot C_{validar}),& \text{si la poda reduce el árbol}\end{cases}

content.text: In the worst case, b is the branching factor (average number of children per node) and d is the depth of the tree. Pruning seeks to ensure that the nodes visited are much less than the theoretical total bd.

blocks.title: Typical height for N-Queens
blocks.latex: T(n)=\begin{cases}O(n^n\cdot n),& \text{si se permite repetir columnas y validar cuesta }O(n)\\O(n!\cdot n),& \text{si se evita repetir columnas y validar cuesta }O(n)\\O(n!),& \text{si columnas y diagonales se validan en }O(1)\end{cases}

content.text: The cost n! It appears when we avoid repeating columns. If we also validate in constant O(1) time, the cost is simply reduced to the number of nodes in the factor tree.

blocks.title: Pruning does not automatically change the worst case

content.text: Just because the algorithm prunes many branches in small examples does not mean that the worst case is no longer exponential or factorial. To change the elevation, you must formally justify how many nodes are eliminated.

content.text: Although the search tree is still large, real-time can be greatly improved by reducing the cost of validating candidates and ordering candidates in a more useful way.
Using Boolean arrays for columns and diagonals (identified by row+col and row-col), we can know if a square is threatened in constant O(1) time, without needing to traverse previous queens.
